name: Strength training (weight and resistance training)
origin: Lifting heavy things to get stronger is ancient, but modern progressive resistance training was developed from 1945 by US Army physician Thomas DeLorme to rehabilitate injured World War II servicemen, and a 1987 trial by Doyne and colleagues was among the first to test weight lifting as a treatment for depression.
summary: Strength training means making your muscles work against a load, such as free weights, machines, resistance bands or your own body weight, usually in sets of about 6 to 15 repetitions with short rests in between. The load is raised gradually as you get stronger, a principle called progressive overload. Unlike HIIT and endurance training, the main aim is stronger muscles rather than keeping the heart rate up, yet trials show it can also ease symptoms of depression and anxiety.
theoryOfChange: Getting measurably stronger week by week gives repeated, concrete proof that effort pays off, which may build confidence and a sense of mastery. Yet in a 2018 meta-analysis the mood benefit did not depend on whether strength improved significantly, and in a 1987 trial weight lifting eased depression about as well as running, so the effect seems to rest on more than bigger muscles or a fitter heart. Brain growth factors, lower inflammation and better sleep are also proposed as routes, but none is proven.
whatYouDo: A session usually starts with a light warm-up, then 6 to 10 exercises covering the main muscle groups, such as squats, push-ups or presses, rows or pull-downs, and hip hinges like deadlifts, each for 2 to 3 sets with a minute or two of rest between sets. You pick a weight that feels hard by the last few repetitions while keeping good form through a full range of motion, and add weight or repetitions as it gets easier. It can be done in a gym, at home with bands or body weight, alone, with a coach or in a class.
typicalDose: At least 2 sessions a week that work all major muscle groups at moderate or greater effort (the WHO 2020 minimum, also advised by ACSM), each often 30 to 60 minutes; heavier loads (about 80% or more of the most you can lift once) tend to build the most strength. Programs in the 2018 depression meta-analysis averaged 16 weeks (range 6 to 52), and the benefit did not depend on program length, frequency, intensity or total training volume.
keyTechniques: Progressive overload: add weight or repetitions over time
Compound lifts such as squats, deadlifts, presses and rows
Sets of about 6 to 15 repetitions with rest between sets
Good technique through a full range of motion
Each major muscle group at least twice a week
Free weights, machines, bands or body weight

evidence.summary: A 2018 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis (Gordon and colleagues, 33 randomized trials, 1,877 adults) found that resistance training reduced depressive symptoms by a moderate amount, with larger benefits in trials of people whose scores indicated mild to moderate depression, and a 2017 meta-analysis by the same team (16 studies, 922 people) found a smaller but consistent reduction in anxiety. A 2024 BMJ network meta-analysis of 218 trials in people with major depression found that strength training gave moderate reductions compared with active control conditions (effect size 0.49) and, with yoga, was the most acceptable form of exercise, but it rated confidence in that result very low because only one of its trials had a low risk of bias. The limits: participants always know they are exercising, effects were smaller in trials with blinded allocation or assessment, results varied widely between trials, and the 2018 review compared training only with inactive control groups, not with medication or therapy.

goodFitFor: People who like clear, measurable goals, dislike long cardio sessions, or want to stay strong and capable as they age, including people with mild to moderate depressive symptoms. It needs little space or equipment, and trials found it well tolerated.
cautions: Poor technique or adding weight too fast can strain muscles, joints and the lower back, so beginners benefit from instruction and gradual progression. Heavy lifting, especially with breath-holding, briefly pushes blood pressure very high (in a classic 1985 study of experienced lifters, peaks averaged 320/250 mmHg during heavy leg presses), so people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, recent heart problems or serious eye disease such as advanced diabetic retinopathy should get medical advice first. A strong focus on size or appearance can sometimes feed body image worries, muscle dysmorphia or anabolic steroid use, which call for professional help.
namingNote: The request listed this point as strength sport with weights. It covers resistance training in general (free weights, machines, bands and body weight), because the mood research pools these together, and competitive lifting such as powerlifting fits inside it. Steady cardio is the endurance point and interval cardio is the HIIT point.
